titre: The Maski Edict (1915): Proof That Piyadasi Was Indeed Ashoka
accroche: Before 1915, no inscription of Ashoka bore his name: all of them said only “Devanampiya Piyadasi.”
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1837, the orientalist James Prinsep managed to decipher the Brahmi script, and dozens of inscriptions carved on pillars and rocks, scattered from present-day Afghanistan to Tamil Nadu, suddenly became legible. All of them celebrate a ruler concerned with morality and nonviolence, but none names him. The text says only “Devanampiya Piyadasi,” “Beloved of the Gods, who looks on everyone with kindness.” For the Buddhist chronicles, composed centuries later in Sri Lanka (the *Mahavamsa*) or in Sanskrit (the *Ashokavadana*), the great ruler who converted to Buddhism after the Kalinga war is named Ashoka. Nothing, before the 20th century, formally linked the two names.

## A Mining Engineer, and a Missing Line

In 1915, C. Beadon, a British mining engineer, discovered an inscription on the rock outcrop of Durgada-gudda, near the village of Maski, in what is now the Raichur district of Karnataka. The text, in Prakrit and in Brahmi script, begins with a formula that no one had yet found elsewhere: the honorific title and the personal name appear side by side, “Devanampiya Asoka.” It is the first time that an inscription explicitly connects the two. The Maski edict has since been corroborated by another minor edict discovered at Gujarra, which bears the same association, “Devanampiya Piyadasi Asokaraja,” so the conclusion does not rest on a single stone.

## What This Shifts

Most archaeological rediscoveries serve to dismantle a received account. This one does the opposite: it finally confirms, directly, an identification that it had until then been reasonable to doubt. Associating the emperor of the edicts (known from official, contemporary inscriptions scattered over an immense territory) with the hero of the Buddhist chronicles, written centuries after his death in a genre that blithely mixes history and religious edification, was not obvious. The skepticism of the first epigraphists was not pedantry: nothing, in the internal coherence of the two corpora alone, required that they speak of the same man.

What settled it was not a philological argument but a stone found by chance, almost eighty years after Prinsep had made the inscriptions legible. Between the decipherment of the script and the proof of the identity, one had to wait for a mining engineer, looking for something else entirely, to stumble on the right line.

repere.texte: Discovered in 1915 by the British mining engineer C. Beadon on the outcrop of Durgada-gudda, near Maski (Karnataka), the edict associates for the first time the title “Devanampiya” with the personal name “Asoka”: an identification since corroborated by the minor edict of Gujarra, which bears the same association.
repere.source: E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, vol. I, Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1925

carte.punch: Before 1915, no one could prove that Ashoka and Piyadasi were the same man.
carte.idee: Ashoka's edicts, legible since 1837, never named him: only the title “Devanampiya Piyadasi” appeared in them. The Buddhist chronicles, for their part, speak of an emperor Ashoka. In 1915, a mining engineer discovers at Maski the first inscription that associates the two.

quiz.question: Why did the identification of Ashoka with the “Devanampiya Piyadasi” inscriptions remain uncertain until 1915?
choix: Because Ashoka's inscriptions had been destroyed before they were deciphered
Because no known inscription associated the honorific title with a personal name, before the Maski discovery
Because historians doubted that the Brahmi script had ever been used in India
Because the Buddhist chronicles placed Ashoka in a different country from the one of the inscriptions
quiz.explication: The inscriptions, legible since 1837, bore only the titles “Devanampiya Piyadasi”; none named the ruler before the Maski edict, the first to associate this title with the name “Asoka.”

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who discovered the Maski inscription, in 1915?
choix: The orientalist James Prinsep, at the end of his decipherment of Brahmi
A French archaeologist, during an official excavation campaign
A British mining engineer, C. Beadon, on a rock outcrop
A Sri Lankan Buddhist monk, following the account of the Mahavamsa
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It was a mining engineer, C. Beadon, who discovered it on the outcrop of Durgada-gudda. Prinsep had only made the inscriptions legible in 1837, seventy-eight years earlier.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the minor edict of Gujarra show in relation to that of Maski?
choix: It contradicts Maski by giving the ruler a different personal name
It bears the same association between the title and the name, and corroborates Maski
It is the first edict to have been deciphered by James Prinsep
It proves that the Buddhist chronicles were written during the king's lifetime
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Gujarra also bears the association “Devanampiya Piyadasi Asokaraja”: the conclusion drawn from Maski therefore does not rest on a single stone.
